To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
surgeons with acute stress symptoms after a surgical complication are at higher risk of post-traumatic symptoms 6 months later.

surgeons who experienced major complications had higher rates of acute stress disorder (ASD) than those who had no complications and that surgeons with ASD had higher rates of post-traumatic distress disorder (PTSD) at 6 months.

the majority of surgeons who experience a major surgical complication develop symptoms of acute traumatic stress, that the severity of these symptoms is associated with the extent of patient injury and death, and that the symptoms can be reduced by discussing the event with colleagues, seeking to learn from the event and to improve one's practice, and avoiding selfdistraction.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a major complication is an emotionally traumatic experience for the responsible surgeon, but that it does not need to be a career-ender.
this study is a first step toward understanding the emotional impact of major complications on surgeons.
the study of Pinto et al. provides an important initial insight into the nature of the stress response of surgeons to major complications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of distraction as a means of dealing with a major complication is associated with increasing symptomatology and the use of self-reflection, self-improvement, and sharing the event with colleagues is associated with decreasing symptomatology.
the use of a ‘‘systems approach’’ to dealing with major surgical complications is associated with less acute traumatic stress.
we have found a new way to treat the disease of cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
surgeons should be aware that they are not immune to the effects of trauma and should seek help when necessary.
the surgeon’s response to the patient’s death is important and can be a source of resilience or a source of distress.
we need to be more open to discussing our experiences with colleagues, and to seek out opportunities for self-improvements.
